structure_rationale: Skill-building: the graph model is the foundation, then each command is a harder question answered with the same model.

chapters.entering_question: What is git actually storing when I commit?
chapters.central_claim_or_skill: A commit is a full snapshot plus parent pointers, so history is a directed graph of snapshots.
chapters.why_it_matters_now: Every later question is 'which node in the graph changed this line', which only makes sense once history is a graph, not a list.
chapters.running_example_or_scene: A developer opens GitHub blame on a config line, clicks through six 'previous blame' views, and loses the thread.
chapters.framework_or_process: Draw the commit graph for a 4-commit repo; show a commit as snapshot + parent(s).
chapters.likely_objection: 'I was told git stores diffs.' Answer: it presents diffs, it stores snapshots; the diff is computed on demand.
chapters.practical_takeaway: Run git cat-file -p HEAD on your own repo and read the tree and parent lines.
chapters.reader_can_now: explain what a commit snapshot contains and why git history is a graph rather than a list
chapters.distinct_from_neighbours: This chapter builds no query skill; it only installs the model the other two chapters use.
chapters.through_line_transition: Once history is a graph of snapshots, the first real question is which snapshot changed a line's content, and one command is built exactly for that.

chapters.working_title: Finding when a line's content changed
chapters.entering_question: This line has a bug. When did it get this way, and why?
chapters.central_claim_or_skill: git log -S finds commits that add or remove a token; git log -L follows a line range through history.
chapters.why_it_matters_now: This is the question that sends developers to click-through GUI blame; it is answerable in one command.
chapters.running_example_or_scene: A timeout constant is wrong; git log -S'TIMEOUT_MS' shows the two commits that ever touched it and the PR reasoning in the messages.
chapters.framework_or_process: Pickaxe for 'when did this token appear/disappear'; -L for 'show me this line's whole life with diffs'.
chapters.likely_objection: '-S missed my change.' Answer: -S counts occurrences; use -G for a regex match on any change to the line.
chapters.practical_takeaway: Pick a suspicious line in your repo and run both git log -S and git log -L on it.
chapters.reader_can_now: use git log -S and git log -L to find the commit that introduced or removed a specific line and read its reasoning
chapters.distinct_from_neighbours: Chapter 1 gave no query; chapter 3 answers a different question (who last touched it, and what was there before) using a different command.
chapters.through_line_transition: log -S and -L tell you when a line changed, but not cleanly who owns its current form or what the line looked like just before; blame does both.

chapters.working_title: Finding who last touched a line and what came before
chapters.entering_question: Who wrote this line as it stands, and what did it replace?
chapters.central_claim_or_skill: git blame gives the last commit per line; blame --reverse finds the last commit a line survived into, which locates when a line was removed.
chapters.why_it_matters_now: Attribution and 'what was here before' are the follow-up questions once you know a line is suspect.
chapters.running_example_or_scene: A log line vanished from production; git blame --reverse on the old commit shows the exact commit that deleted it.
chapters.framework_or_process: blame for current ownership; blame --reverse for 'when did this disappear'; -w/-M/-C to see through noise.
chapters.likely_objection: 'Blame just shows a formatting commit.' Answer: add -w to ignore whitespace and -M/-C to see through moves.
chapters.practical_takeaway: Run git blame -w on a file you know was reformatted, with and without -w, and compare.
chapters.reader_can_now: use git blame and git blame --reverse to trace a line backward to its author and forward to the commit that removed it
chapters.distinct_from_neighbours: Chapter 2 answered 'when did the content change'; this answers 'who owns it now' and 'when did it leave', which -S and -L do not do directly.
chapters.through_line_transition: With all three commands in hand, the last step is choosing among them quickly, which the closing checklist makes mechanical.
